# Lab Notebook

This document contains the basic record of experiments and runs for two
dimensional molecular dynamics simulation.

The code was started in *Mathematica* in early 2024, but that was
abandoned when it became clear that it was too hard to debug C code
being run from within *Mathematica*. Investigated a few possible
alternatives, and decided on *Julia* as the best language to do high
performance computing.

The first check-in was on 23 May 2024. The first full run with stable
potential energy was a month later.

# Runs From Initialization

The first series of runs were from initialization, which was simpler
than the 1980 Thesis code. The 1980 code used a technique described as
"one which would be expected of an harmonic lattice (this is seen to
during the process of disturbing the system)"[@Shea1980]. The current
code simply starts the system in its rest position, giving each particle
Gaussian velocities in each direction. The total energy is thus divided
into potential energy as the system runs. No heating or cooling was
implemented yet in the *Julia* code.

## Series 1

The first run of the system was on 18 July 2024. This series is
documented in
[Data-OverviewS1.pdf](file:///home/phil/MD/MD/MD2/Data-OverviewS1.pdf){.pdf},
archived on 1 August. The result was a possible location for the
transition region. 300 runs were made, with initialization setting the
mean temperatures of the particles from 0.001 to 0.300. Each run
consisted of an initialization run of 1,000 steps, followed by two 5,000
step runs, so 11,000 steps total. There have been some changes to the
*Julia* code since this was run, but the initialization was essentially
like the code below.

```{julia}
#| eval: false
   ss.v .= randn( eltype( ss.v), ss.N)
   # each dimension has energy kT / 2 = V^2 / 2, E[V^2]=T
   ss.v .= sqrt( Temp) .* ss.v
```

where `Temp` was the initialization temperature. Note that the total
energy includes the potential energy at rest. The nearest neighbors are
at a distance of $a = \sqrt{\pi / \sin(\pi / 3)} \approx 1.90463$. The
second nearest neighbors are at a distance of
$a \sqrt{3} \approx 3.2989$. So the initial potential energy is one half
of the energy between each particle. $1 / a^5 \approx .039898$, and the
second nearest neighbor energy is $1 / (a\sqrt{3})^5 \approx .0025594$.
Summing these and multiplying by three (half of six) yields a per
particle potential energy at rest of $0.127373$.

The complete summary is below in @fig-allS1. Each item is a summary of
the 10,000 steps following the 1,000 steps after initialization. The
data is in `MD2DF.S1.Rdata`.

![Summary of all S1 data.](images\S1AllSummary.PNG){#fig-allS1}

The `r.squared` response identified an area of interest. A zoomed in
plot of kinetic energy (i.e., temperature) versus total energy is below
in fig-allS1z.

![Kinetic Energy vs. mean Total Energy for series
1.](images/S1kevsTE.PNG){#fig-allS1z}

It was also apparent that there were large gaps in the total energy even
though the energies were initialized incrementally. This was suspected
to be due to the random nature of the initialization, where the total
energy was simply the variance of 512 (i.e., $256 * 2$) random normal
deviates.

The initial data ran some very hot runs, so a plot zoomed into the
transition region is below in @fig-S1summary.

![Zoomed in summary of S1 data in
@fig-allS1.](images/S1Summary.PNG){#fig-S1summary}

It was also noted that this series did not zero the angular momentum at
initialization. While angular momentum is not conserved by the periodic
boundary conditions, no good can come of initializing a run with angular
momentum.

### Spectral Processing

The kinetic energy line appeared to have some spectral content, and this
may prove interesting. Spectral estimation code was already available,
and the following was executed (`x` was a data frame returned from
`combineruns`, which creates a data frame of each variables as columns,
and each step as rows):

```{r}
#| eval: false
sx36 <- detrend( tail( x[, "ke"], -2000)) # remove mean and linear trend
x36sdf <- qsdf(sx36, blocksize=4096, yrange=110, dt=0.01)
```

As is evident, the first 2,000 points was skipped. The `qsdf` function
will break the signal into overlapping blocks of `blocksize`, with 50%
overlap being the default. The default is also to apply a Hanning
window. With only 9,000 points (after skipping 2k), the spectrum is only
3 blocks long. Note that the plot in `Data Overview S2.pdf` appears to
be incorrect; the correct plot is @fig-S20036fspec below:

![Full spectrum of run S2.0036 less the first 2k
points.](images/x36spec.png){#fig-S20036fspec}

Zooming in (@fig-S20036fspecz) we can see the following:

![The blue lines contain 99% of the signals
power.](images/x36%20spec%20zoom.png){#fig-S20036fspecz}

The blue lines are at $\pm 0.708/\tau$ for a main lobe width of
$1.416/\tau$. Since the sample rate is $0.01\tau$, the spectral width is
the equivalent of about 70 samples. To create a block average which will
encompass that, it would have to be at least twice that wide (as the
null-to-null bandwidth of main lobe of the average is twice the
reciprocal of the block average size).

#### Detour on Regression

A surprising plot was made of the regression slope estimate divided by
the standard error of that estimate, plotted against the regression
coefficient. This turned out to be a parabola, which was surprising. A
complete investigation revealed that this was an artifact of how the
data was produced. This is all documented in
[Regression_Ratios.pdf](file://home/phil/MD/MD/RegressionRatios/Regression_Ratios.pdf),
a paper written in LaTeX on
[Overleaf](https://www.overleaf.com/project). Ultimately decided on
using the $t$ statistic to decide if a run had no real slope, generally
using a 50% confidence interval (that is, if the confidence that the
slope was zero was 50% or greater, it would be considered valid
equilibrium).

### Re-sampling and Autocorrelation

Experience from 1980 and the results reported in [@Novaco1982] indicates
that we need to use average temperatures and pressures to decide if we
have reached equilibrium. In 1980, we we used 1k samples as it was the
basic simulation block, but today I would like a more rational answer.
The autocorrelation of four runs was examined to see what should be
done.

::: {#tbl-AutoCorr4tb}
| Symbol Name | File Name | Mean KE | $r^2$  | Mean TE |
|------------:|:---------:|:-------:|:------:|:-------:|
|         x10 |  S2.0010  | 0.0047  | 0.0003 | 0.1364  |
|        xn02 |  S2.0033  | 0.0154  | 0.1931 | 0.1615  |
|         x36 |  S2.0036  | 0.0146  | 0.2887 | 0.1591  |
|        x100 |  S2.0100  | 0.0499  | 0.0230 | 0.2242  |

: Summary of autocorrelation runs

![Auto-correlations of the four series in
@tbl-AutoCorr4tb.](images/four%20Autocorr.png){#fig-Autocorr4fig}

### Updating `runcombiner.r`

The *Julia* code produces step-by-step data in blocks of steps. This is
for two reasons: 1) a run may need to be extended, and so another block
of data could be added to existing runs, rather than starting over from
the beginning, and 2) stuff, happens, and if a million steps is desired,
experience has shown that having data written to "disk" occasionally is
wise. This second reason may seem silly when a thousand steps can be run
in .16 seconds, but as the size of the system is expanded, this will
become important. Nevertheless, that is how the code is structured, and
so the steps must be combined. This was done in R, as of this writing in
a single file named `runcombiner.R`. The record of this is in
[UpdatetoRuncombiner.pdf](file:///C:/Users/phils/My%20Drive/DSP/MD/UpdatetoRuncombiner.pdf).

The re-sampled data with a regression on the last 2/3 of the data is
represented in @fig-x33resamp below:

![Fits to the re-sampled data, the red line is the fit to all of the
data (red and blue circles), and the last two-thirds of truncated run
S2-0033 (blue circles and line). Green lines indicate the mean (solid),
and min & max (dashed) of the blue points. The black line is the
regression line for the red
points.](images/x33resamp.png){#fig-x33resamp}

The algorithm to determine if a run has reached equilibrium is below (in
seven easy steps):

1.  Skip the first 1,000 points as a general rule.
2.  Re-sample the kinetic energy (`ke`) column.
3.  Regress the re-sampled column, and check if the F statistic p-value
    is below 50% (that is, if the data were truly random and
    uncorrelated, there is a 50% chance that we would reject the large
    the data set and and move to the next step). If it passes the
    F-test, accept the data as uncorrelated, and compute the averages
    for the rest of the columns.
4.  Having failed the first F-test, take the last two-thirds of the
    data, and repeat the F-test. If this fails, then a longer run is
    needed (i.e., we require that equilibrium be at least twice as long
    as the approach to equilibrium). At this point, simply report the
    full record's averages, and let the statistics indicate the record's
    problem.
5.  If the second F-test passes, then compute the mean, min, and max of
    the two-thirds data, and also compute the regression of the first
    third. This second regression will give the direction of the
    temperature movement.
6.  Find the last point outside the min or max of the two-thirds data.
    If the second regression has a positive coefficient (i.e., the ke is
    rising), use the min, and use the max otherwise.
7.  Perform a third regression on the new set of points. If the F-test
    fails, then resort to the original two-thirds data. If the use the
    F-test passes, use the expanded data set for the averages.

The above has been encapsulated in the `findlmlen` function, and
incorporated into the `createdf` function. A rather large amount of work
went into extending the last two thirds back into the series, so an
experiment was run on random data. The following *R* code was the
experiment (displayed here because of its simplicity):

```{r}
#| eval: false
len <- 50
(len3 <- floor(len/3))
trials <- 10000
q <- t( # need to transpose the result of replicate
   replicate( trials, findlmlen( data.frame( step = 1:len, ke = rnorm( len)))))
```

This generated 10,000 length 50 series of random data and ran
`findlmlen` on them. The results are in @tbl-findlmtst below.

::: {#tbl-findlmtst}
|               Item | Count  | Percent |
|-------------------:|:------:|:-------:|
|       Total Trials | 10,000 |  100%   |
| Full Length Passes | 5,007  |  50.1%  |
|   Shortened Passes | 2,231  |  22.3%  |
|        Exactly 2/3 |  393   |  3.9%   |
|  Lengthened Passes | 1,838  |  18.4%  |
|      Failed Passes | 2,762  |  27.6%  |

: Results of `findlmlen` on random data.
:::

The first thing to notice: the expected number of full length passes is
50%, and this was observed. Of the 2,231 shortened passes, 82% were
lengthened. The 1/3 length is given by `len3 <- floor( 50/3)` which is
16. The 2/3 length is $50 - 16 = 34$. The average length of the
shortened runs was 34.88, so it looks like most runs were only
lengthened by 1 point. The maximum short pass was 38 (lengthened by 4).
A plot of the result is below in @fig-regtest.

![Absolute value of the estimate vs. the standard error for 10,000
trials of length 50 regressions. Black points are failures, green are
full length passes, and blue are shortened passes. The red line shows
equality (estimate equals the standard
error).](images/findlmlentst.PNG){#fig-regtest}

There were two iterations, with the final summarization of the data
performed with re-sampling block size of 500. The updated summary data
is in `MD2DF.3.S2.Rdata`. The summary plot of the data is in

![Summary of data in MD2DF.3.S2.Rdata. The red triangles are data runs

![Eight key parameters, the first six (counting top-to-bottom,

The Nelson-Halperin order parameter
$\psi = \frac{1}{2(N-1)}\sum_{i \ne j} e^{i6\theta_{i j}}$, where
$\theta_{i j}$ is the angle with the $x$-axis of the vector from
particle $i$ to $j$ (the factor of 2 because in the above, each particle
is counted twice). This is very sensitive to the transition.
@fig-NHOPER1 below shows the current state with $\pm\sigma$ error band.

![The Nelson-Halperin order parameter versus TE (energy in scaled
units). Red triangles denote points not considered
valid.](images/NHOPER1.png){#fig-NHOPER1 width="700"}

We assume that the runs below $0.155\epsilon$ belong to the frozen
(solid phase) systems, and the valid runs above $0.165\epsilon$ belong
to the fluid phase. Linear fits to the two regions result in the lines
in @fig-LinFitsphaseER1:

![Linear fits to solid (black) and fluid (blue)
phases.](images/LinFitphaseER1.png){#fig-LinFitsphaseER1}

### Update Initialization Code

The next series of runs needs to extend the runs elicited above, plus
fill in the energies that are missing. The `InitMDRecord!` function was
updated to zero in on the energies in a better way. Previously, the
energy was set as a parameter to the random number generation, but the
random generation could result in many different energies. The old code
was as follows:

```{julia}
#| eval: false
    ss.v .= sqrt( Temp) .* randn( eltype( ss.v), ss.N)
```

The new code is as follows:

```{julia}
#| eval: false
    ss.v .= randn( eltype( ss.v), ss.N)
    ke = 0.5 * sum( dot.(ss.v, ss.v)) / ss.N
    ss.v .= sqrt( Temp / ke) .* ss.v
```

As can be seen, the random numbers are generated first, and then they
are scaled to meet the temperature. It is still not exact, as linear and
angular momentum are corrected after the kinetic energy generation, and
this does change it a bit, but it ought to be a lot closer now.

### Melting!

Over 13 & 14 October 2024, extended a few runs to over one million
steps. There where a few runs which stood out: one which had not reached
equilibrium when the runs at energies above and below it did, and one
which reached equilibrium when the runs above and below it did not. On
21 October, this caused me to look at the `S2b.0027` run in detail. This
first revealed that the `combineruns` routine had an error, in which the
sort by `file.time` was silently failing, and the runs were jumbled. The
entire notebook `ExtendRuns2.qmd` is invalid now, although a re-run may
give odd results. It will be re-run and archived.

Nevertheless, in this process, run `S2b.0027` was examined and
@fig-S2b0027 was the result.

![Run S2b.0027 after one million steps. Melting is most obvious in the
imaginary component of the Nelson-Halperin order parameter (Impsi) after
time $6,000\tau$ (600k
steps).](images/Mainscalarsx271M.png){#fig-S2b0027 width="600"}

We can see that the total energy is decreasing, which might be
concerning. The reduction is 0.8%. This is likely due to particles
slipping out of the `rskn` range of the potential. Note that
simultaneously, the potential energy (`pe`) is increasing and the
kinetic energy (`ke`) is decreasing.

## Nelson-Halperin Order Parameter

There are two metrics recorded: `psiavg` and `psiabs.mean.rs`. The
parameter is reported step-by-step as as real and imaginary components
of the base parameter. Its calculation is as follows:

$$\psi_s = \frac{1}{N_q} \sum_{j = 1}^{N_p} \sum_{k \ near\ j} e^{i 6 \theta_{j,k}}$$

where $s$ is the step number, $N_p$ are the number of particles,
$k \ near\ j$ means the particles "near" particle $j$ such that $k > j$
(and near is simply defined as less than 3/2 of the mean inter-particle
distance, a constant in the calculation), and $\theta_{j,k}$ is the
angle between the x-axis and the vector between particles $j$ and $k$.
$N_q$ is the count of those particles that met the $k\ near\ j$
criteria. $\psi_s$ is a complex quantity whose magnitude indicates the
average alignment of the particles (and is the fourier coefficient of
6-fold spacing). Since we have the step-by-step value of $\psi_s$, we
can perform the average two ways. Perhaps the obvious is to compute the
magnitude of $\psi_s$ and then average that. This is
$\langle |\psi_s| \rangle$, where the magnitude is computed at each step
(and that is what is plotted step-by-step in `plotMD2`). The analogy to
Fourier estimation is supported by this technique, in which multiple
spectrums taken at different times are averaged in magnitude. The other
value we can compute is the magnitude of the average, or
$|\langle \psi_s \rangle|$. The spectral analogy is of the magnitude of
a single high resolution Fourier coefficient They are both plotted in
@fig-bothpsi below.

![Plots of $\langle |\psi_s| \rangle$ (red open symbols) and
$|\langle \psi_s \rangle|$ (blue closed symbols). Circles are points
considered valid, and triangles are those points not considered valid.
The solid samples overlap.](images/bothpsi.png){#fig-bothpsi}

There is little doubt that $\theta$ is rotating in some samples. We
actually saw this in run `S2b.0027`. @fig-xn27anglez2 below is a plot of
the angle and magnitude of $\langle \psi \rangle_{N_q}$, there the
notation is to indicate that each point is an average over the $N_q$
particles.

![Plot of the angle and magnitude of a small portion of the `S2b.0027`
run. The angle is $(30/\pi) Arg(\psi)$, so we can see an approximate
angle of $\theta$. The steps above are divided by 1,000, and the time
index is $0.01\tau$ per step, so times may be determined by multiplying
by 10 (13,050 to
13,300$\tau$).](images/xn27anglez2.png){#fig-xn27anglez2}

# New Definition of Validity

The previous definition was using any $F_p > 0.5$ as indication of
validity. The reason being that if perfectly random data had greater
than a 50% chance of causing that observation, any trend was likely
spurious. However, we see that when millions of steps are run,
regression will report that the slope is minuscule with high
significance (thus, very small $F_p$). These cases are just as valid. So
the new criteria will combine the two: $F_p > 0.5$ or the estimated
slope is *small* with with significance (say, 95%). We define *small* as
an error of less than 20% of the standard deviation of the temperature.
Unfortunately, we must re-run all of the files through `procMD2DF` to
accomplish this. We could probably just run the invalid files, but is is
possible, although unlikely, that the regression length will change with
the expanded criteria. (it is unlikely because of the required small
slope estimate will not likely be significant without many points.)

The code snippet below shows that all but four would be valid.

```{r}
#| eval: false
nv <- !with( MD2DF.B[ MD2DF.B$Fpvalue < 0.5,], 
      (Estimate * steps.avg / 2 < 0.2 * ke.sd.rs) & (Fpvalue <= 0.05))
MD2DF.B[ MD2DF.B$Fpvalue < 0.5,][nv, 
                     .(run, TE.mean.rs, Estimate, Fpvalue, ke.sd.rs, steps.avg)]
```

| Run | Mean Total Energy | Slope Estimate | Fp Value | ke standard deviation | Steps in Averages |
|----|----|----|----|----|----|
| S2b.0026 | 0.15246 | 1.1643e-08 | 0.00075 | 0.00026185 | 2,050,000 |
| S2b.0032 | 0.15834 | -3.5342e-09 | 0.4517 | 0.00038216 | 2,150,000 |
| S2.0033 | 0.16146 | 5.1504e-09 | 0.2348 | 0.00033092 | 2,060,000 |
| S2.0039 | 0.16786 | 1.3377e-06 | 0.1996 | 0.00039460 | 60,000 |

The next step here is to upgrade `procMD2DF`, and update the plotting
algorithms to deal with a `valid` tag vs. simply filtering on `Fpvalue`.

## New Definitions Applied

Unexpectedly, the procedure outlined above produced the pathological
result that only the *steepest* sloped lines were significant enough to
be declared valid. @fig-estfail is an example of a simulation of 10,000
length 4,000 normally distributed random numbers. In that figure, it is
evident that the steepest lines are accepted.

![Absolute value of the estimate vs. the standard error. Black points
are failures, green are full length passes, blue are shortened passes,
and the red points are those added where the regression line ends 20% or
less than the standard deviation. The red line shows equality (estimate
equals the standard error).](images/estvstderrflm2.png){#fig-estfail}

So this procedure is considered a failure, and the final resolution was
to drop back to that used in [@Shea1980], where the slope had to be less
than the standard error of the slope (the equivalent of the red line in
@fig-estfail. This is the equivalent of the $F$-test value being less
than one and will happen anywhere from 68.8% to 68.3% of normally
distributed data as the number of samples (i.e., the $F$ distribution
second degree-of-freedom parameter) ranges from 50 to 4,000.

# Transition

The low energy end of the transition region itself is somewhat
arbitrarily declared as the total energy of run `S2.0029` (which also
functions as the highest energy of the solid region). We therefore
define the transition region to start at total energy of
$0.15352\epsilon$. The 18 data points that make up this mean total
energy have a small standard deviation of $3.84 \times 10^{-5} \epsilon$
(a mere 0.025%). The two regression lines appear straight (but the fluid
line is not straight), and properly weighted regressions are performed
on them (weighted regressions performed above ignored the number of
points used in the averages; regressions performed below used weights
defined as $N/\sigma^2$, where N is the number of points in the average,
and $\sigma$ is the standarad deviation of the 500-point resampled
avereages). The solid line assumes a minimum energy of
$0.127373\epsilon$, which is the potential energy of the particles in
their minimum energy positions. (Note that this is about 3.7% high, as
the calculation has the potential step at the skin range of $3.5\sigma$,
an addition which shows up int the potential energy calculation, but is
ignored in the force calculations.) The solid line regression estimates
only the slope, as the the zero temperature point occurs at the minimum
energy.

The fluid line is defined as by *all* points (declared valid or not)
above total energy of $0.157 \epsilon$, a value chosen because it lies
between points we want to exclude and those we want to include. The fit
is to 79 points.

The right side of the transition region is defined by the intersection
of the fluid regression line with the prediction of the solid line at
the total energy of `S2.0029`, thus, not the measured temperature of
$0.013152 \epsilon$, but the predicted ($0.013563 \epsilon$).

drawn between (intersecting) the two regression lines. $1\sigma$

along with the regression lines, as well as gray region showing the

Regressions were weighted with $\sigma^2/N$, where $N$ is the number of

## Thermodynamic Scaling

The $r^{-n}$ potential allows us to create isobars (constant pressure)
or isotherms (constant temperature) from our constant density
simulations. The important thermodynamic variable is
$\eta = \rho \sigma^2 \left( \epsilon / k T \right)^{2/n}$, where $\rho$
is the density, $T$ is the temperature, and $\sigma$, $\epsilon$ and $k$
are the distance unit, energy unit, and Boltzmann's constant
respectively, and all are defined as one, which of course means that
$\rho$ and $T$ are in scaled units [@Shea1980; @Novaco1982]. Also, the
pressure and temperature scale such that
$P_1 / \rho_1 T_1 = P_2 / \rho_2 T_2$ (this is the equivalent of the
[Ideal Gas Law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ideal_gas_law) in two
dimensions). If we want to draw an isobar or isotherm curve, we need use
the scaling to map the measurements to different scales. If we have
measurement $T_1$ at pressure $P_1$ and density $\rho_1$, we can map to
a new pressure $P_2$ via

$$T_2 = \frac{\rho_1 T_1 P_2}{\rho_2 P_1}$$

Then we use the fact that
$\eta = \rho_1 / T_1^{2/n} = \rho_2 / T_2^{2/n}$ to replace $\rho_2$ in
the above yielding

\begin{align*}
T_2 &= \frac{\rho_1 T_1 P_2}{P_1 \eta T_2^{2/n}} \\
    &= \frac{\rho_1 T_1 P_2}{ P_1 \left(\rho_1 / T_1^{2/n}\right) T_2^{2/n}} \\
T_2^{1 + 2/n} &= \frac{T_1^{1 + 2/n} P_2}{P_1} \\
T_2 &= T_1 \left( P_2/P_1 \right)^{\left( 1 / (1 + 2/n) \right)} 
\end{align*}

That's messy, but now that we have a $T_2$, and density
$\rho_2 = \rho_1 P_2 T_1 / P_1 T_2$. The following code executes that
plot (@fig-isobar).

```{r}
#| label: fig-isobar
#| eval: false
#| output: true
with( MD2DF.C, {
  n <- 5 # current potential exponent
  P2 <- 0.1175 # near transition pressure at 1/pi density
  T2 <- ke.mean.rs * (P2 / Pressure.mean.rs)^( 1 / (1 + (2 / n)))
  den2 <- P2 * ke.mean.rs / (pi * Pressure.mean.rs * T2)
  plotconf( x = (1/den2), y = T2, Fval = Fval, linethresh = 200, 
            panel.first = grid(), xlab = "Area / Particle", 
            ylab = "Temperature")
  axis( side = 1, at = pi, labels = expression(pi))
})
```

![Isobar at $P=0.1175$, the pressure near the transition at $1/\pi$
density (see @fig-pvske).](images/isobar.png){#fig-isobar}

Similar algebra yields the following for a constant temperature
(Isotherm):

\begin{align*}
P_2 &= \frac{P_1 \rho_2 T_2}{\rho_1 T_1} \\
    &= \frac{P_1 \eta T_2^{1 + 2/n}}{\rho_1 T_1} \\
    &= \frac{P_1 \left(\rho_1 / T_1^{n/2}\right)T_2^{1 + 2/n} }{\rho_1 T_1} \\
P_2 &= P_1 \left(\frac{T_2}{T_1}\right)^{1 + 2/n} \label{eq-isotherm}
\end{align*}

The equations above are implemented in the code below to plot
@fig-isotherm.

```{r}
#| label: fig-isotherm
#| eval: false
#| output: true
with( MD2DF.C, {
  n <- 5 # current potential exponent
  T2 <- 0.013 # near transition temp at 1/pi density
  P2 <- Pressure.mean.rs * (T2 / ke.mean.rs)^(1+2/n)
  den2 <- P2 * ke.mean.rs / (pi * Pressure.mean.rs * T2)
  plotconf( x = (1/den2), y = P2, Fval = Fval, linethresh = Inf, 
            panel.first = grid(), xlab = "Area / Particle", ylab = "Pressure")
  axis( side = 1, at = pi, labels = expression(pi))
})
```

![Isotherm at $T=0.013$.](images/isotherm.png){#fig-isotherm}

That plot is surprising, as the formerly very low temperature
measurement ends up in the denominator, requires a very high pressure to
maintain the configuration at the selected temperature of the isotherm.
We can zoom into the transition region and see the subtle change in
pressure (@fig-isotherm2).

![Zoom into transition region of Isotherm at
$T=0.013$.](images/isotherm2.png){#fig-isotherm2}

## Specific Heat

Numerically differentiating the temperature with respect to total energy
allows us to estimate the specific heat. The following code produced
@fig-cv.

```{r}
#| label: fig-Cv
#| eval: false
#| output: true
setkey( MD2DF.C, TE.mean.rs) # Sets sort key.
with( MD2DF.C[valid==1,], {
+     delta <- 2
+     dte <- diff( TE.mean.rs, delta)
+     te2 <- head(TE.mean.rs, -delta) + dte / 2
+     dke <- diff( ke.mean.rs, delta)
+     cvnd <- dte / dke
+     plot( x = te2, y = cvnd, xlab = "Total Energy", ylab = "Specific Heat",
+           panel.first = grid(),xlim= c(0.15,0.165))
+ })
```

![Specific heat estimated by taking the difference between every other
*valid* point. There is a lot of variance in the data, and two points in
the transition region show up as negative as the temperatures decreased
in (perhaps randomly) in the region.](images\Cv.png){#fig-cv
width="60%"}

# Plans for Next Runs

While all this data is valid, there are enough difficulties to suggest
re-running it all. The *Julia* `MD2` code needs to be upgraded with the
following changes.

1.  Remove potential step (count the number of particles interacting and
    subtract step for PE calculation).
2.  Report the number of particles interacting.
3.  Report stats in correlation calculation.
4.  Add diffusion calculation and report.
5.  Add heating/cooling.

The runs themselves need to be better organized.

a)  Come up with a plan for the distribution of initial energies, taking
    specific heat calculations into consideration,
b)  Make the run length dependent on energy, so the temperature variance
    remains the same.
c)  make uniform 4M step runs through the transition region.

## Self Diffusion

The diffusion estimation is given by
$\left< r^2 \right>_t = \left< \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i = 1}^N \left[ \vec{r}_i(t + s) -  \vec{r}_i(s)\right]^2 \right>$
[@Shea1980]

> ...where $N$ is the number of particles, and $s$ is a time used as an
> initial time. The brackets on the right hand side are meant to
> indicate an average over different $s$ (typically, 20 different $s$
> are used, spaced by 250 steps). $\left< r^2 \right>$ is plotted as a
> function of time, and then examined to see if the self diffusion is
> behaving in a linear fashion at long times. If it is, a linear
> regression is performed on this linear portion. The distinction
> between linear and nonlinear diffusion is quite obvious and the
> portion of a configuration showing linear diffusion is easily
> discerned. The three different results which are likely are shown in
> Figure \ref{fig:two}. It is shown in appendix B that
> $\frac{d}{d t} \left< r^2 \right> = 4 D$ in two dimensions.

As of 4 June 2025, most of the above has been accomplished, and a series
three set of data has been run. The machinery to count the number of
particles interacting was never written, but the maximum `Mmax` is
recorded, and the maximum number of interactions (for example, 3,035)
are both printed to the run's `.txt` file. The notes above was using the
data frame `MD2DF.C`, and we are now on `MD2DF.L`. There are now a total
of 198 runs.

| S2     |   100 | Original Runs with angular momentum correction.     |
| S2b    |    13 | Added Init energy correction.                       |
| S3     |    76 | Removed PE step, added diffusion, heating, cooling. |
| S3b    |     9 | These were simply additional S3 runs.               |

relative temperature variance (the variance of the 500-point re-sampled
temperatures divided by the temperature mean), `psiavg` is the magnitude
of the average of $\psi$ (i.e., the average of the complex quantity) and
`psiabs.mean.rs` is the average of the magnitude of $\psi$. `D4` is the
estimate of diffusion computed as $4D$, `Fvald` is the F-value of the
diffusion regression of $\left< R^2(t) \right> \sim t$ (where $t$ is
time; low F-vals indicate that there is no correlation, thus no
diffusion).

![Statistics around transition plotted against temperature. Tan dots are
points considered valid, blue ones not valid. See text for description
of statistics.](images/Transitions.png){#fig-Transition height="9in"
width="6.5in"}

## A Detected Transition *Before* Melting

Finding objective evidence of transitions found a new one. I created a
function that will fit a line to the data and detect when the next point
departs significantly from that line. While we'll show below that the
melting transition is near $T = 0.1283$, a clear but subtle transition
occurs at $T = 0.00797$. This is shown in @fig-icld12507 below.

![Isochor of points up to first detection, plus ten points. Red vertical
dashed line shows the detected point. The 99% confidence interval ends
at $P = 0.101078$ but the point's pressure is
0.010190.](images/icld12507.png){#fig-icld12507}

So we were able to model four states (@fig-S3State).

![Isochor with points colored by
state.](images/S3State.png){#fig-S3State}

Modeling the solid as two regions shows that they have statistically
different specific heats, to a virtual certainty. The model is
$P = \alpha_0 + \beta_0 T + s(\alpha_s +\beta_s T)$, where $s$ is one in
the `Solid2` state and zero otherwise, and $\alpha_0$, $\beta_0$,
$\alpha_s$, and $\beta_s$ are the coefficients of the model. The
regression result below shows the coefficients for that form of the
equation. The result also shows that all coefficients are statistically
highly significant.

```         
Call:
lm(formula = Pressure.mean.rs ~ ke.mean.rs * State, data = S3DTdiff2[State %in% 
    c("Solid1", "Solid2"), ])

Residuals:
      Min        1Q    Median        3Q       Max 
-3.36e-05 -3.45e-06 -8.50e-07  2.72e-06  5.24e-05 

Coefficients:
                        Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept)             9.23e-02   1.11e-05  8338.7  < 2e-16 ***
ke.mean.rs              1.10e+00   2.44e-03   453.0  < 2e-16 ***
StateSolid2            -4.80e-04   4.38e-05   -11.0  2.2e-10 ***
ke.mean.rs:StateSolid2  5.74e-02   4.71e-03    12.2  2.9e-11 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 ‘***’ 0.001 ‘**’ 0.01 ‘*’ 0.05 ‘.’ 0.1 ‘ ’ 1

Residual standard error: 2.04e-05 on 22 degrees of freedom
Multiple R-squared:     1,  Adjusted R-squared:     1 
F-statistic: 3.61e+05 on 3 and 22 DF,  p-value: <2e-16
```

The `S3Analysis.pdf` report also compared the AIC for model 2 (solid
region as one linear equation, and model 6 (solid region as two linear
equations). The AIC for model 2 was -432.72, and for model 6 it was
-482.24, so the two-region model is preferred.

So model 6 (the only one to estimate $\beta_s$ is clearly superior to
almost ten 9's (99.99...99%) certainty. The actual value of the specific
heats can be best garnered from the coefficients of the models of just
those sections (see @tbl-models1). The intercepts are not important and
so not presented in the table (most are available in the code output
above).

::: {#tbl-models1}
| Model | Data | $\beta_0 \pm \sigma_\beta$ ($\beta_s \pm \sigma_{\beta_s}$) |
|----|----|----|
| model1 | `Solid1` | 1.104 $\pm0.04\%$ |
| model2 | `Solid1` & `Solid2` | 1.122 $\pm0.26\%$ |
| model3 | `Solid2` | 1.162 $\pm0.54\%$ |
| model6 | `Solid1` & `Solid2` | 1.104 $\pm0.22\%$, (0.0574 $\pm 8.2\%$) |

significant. Model 1 only modeled the `Solid1` region. Model 2 included

linear coefficients for all four states) are not relevant to these
results.

The `model6` coefficients for `Solid2` (where the two coefficients are
added) differ from that estimated directly in `model3` by only 3.42%.

## Isochor, Isobar, & Isotherm

We will start by reproducing the isochor plot of all points
(@fig-pvske_eta). The isochor is a plot of pressure vs. temperature
(constant density). We re-derived this, and included one significant
change. The $r^{-n}$ potential allows us to create isobars (constant
pressure) or isotherms (constant temperature) from constant density
data. The important thermodynamic variable is
$\eta = \rho \sigma^2 \left( \epsilon / k T \right)^{2/n}$, where $\rho$
is the density, $T$ is the temperature, and $\sigma$, $\epsilon$ and $k$
are the distance unit, energy unit, and Boltzmann's constant
respectively, all are defined as one, meaning $\rho$ and $T$ are in
scaled units [@Shea1980] [@Novaco1982].

![Isochor of all points at density $\rho = 1/\pi$. The blue dashed lines
represent the temperature and pressure of the isotherm and isobar plots
below. The gray lines are lines of constant
$\eta = \rho \left( \epsilon / T \right)^{2/n}$.](images/pvske_eta.png){#fig-pvske_eta}

The above figure was produced with the following *R* code:

```{r}
#| eval: false
#| output: true
#| fig-cap: 'Isochor of all points at density $\rho = 1/\pi$. The blue dashed lines represent the temperature and pressure of the isotherm and isobar plots below.  The gray lines are lines of constant $\eta = \rho \left( \epsilon / T \right)^{2/n}$.'
isotherm <- function( P1, T1, T2, n) {P1 * (T2 / T1)^(1 + 2/n)} # compute P2
isot = 0.0129
isob = 0.1075
plotconfMD2( S3DTdiff2, x = "ke.mean.rs", y = "Pressure", 
             xlab = "Temperature", ylab = "Pressure",
             main = "Isochor of all points with scaling lines", 
            ylim = c( 0.01, 0.15))
abline( h = isob, col= "blue", lty = 2)
abline( v = isot, col= "blue", lty = 2)
  tr <- range( S3DTdiff2$ke.mean.rs) # T1 range
  ts <- seq( tr[1], tr[2], length.out = 200)
  t1s <- isot + c(-0.005, -0.01, 0, 0.005, 0.01, 0.015, 0.02,.025, .03)
  for (T1 in t1s) {
    lines( x = ts, y = isotherm( isob, T1, ts, 5), col = 'gray', lty = 1, 
           lwd = 2)
  }
```

The scaling lines show that when scaling to constant pressure,
temperatures below the constant pressure scale up in temperature, and
those above scale down. Conversely, when scaling to constant
temperature, pressures below the constant temperature scale up in
pressure, and those above scale down, both rather dramatically.

The pressure and temperature scale such that
$P_1 / \rho_1 T_1 = P_2 / \rho_2 T_2$ (this is the equivalent of the
[Ideal Gas Law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ideal_gas_law) in two
dimensions). If we want to draw an isobar or isotherm curve, we need use
the scaling to map the measurements to different scales. If we have a
measurement $T_1$ and pressure $P_1$ at density $\rho_1$ ($1/\pi$ for
us), we can map $T_2$ to a pressure $P_2$ via

$$T_2 = \frac{\rho_1 T_1 P_2}{\rho_2 P_1}$$

Then we use $\eta = \rho_1 / T_1^{2/n} = \rho_2 / T_2^{2/n}$ to replace
$\rho_2 = \rho_1 \left(T_2/ T_1\right)^{2/n}$ in the above yielding

\begin{align*}
T_2 &= \frac{\rho_1 T_1 P_2}{P_1 \eta T_2^{2/n}} \\
    &= \frac{\rho_1 T_1 P_2}{ P_1 \left(\rho_1 / T_1^{2/n}\right) T_2^{2/n}} \\
T_2^{1 + 2/n} &= \frac{T_1^{1 + 2/n} P_2}{P_1} \\
T_2 &= T_1 \left( P_2/P_1 \right)^{\left( 1 / (1 + 2/n) \right)}\\
    &= T_1 \left( \frac{P_2}{P_1} \right)^{\left( n/ (n + 2) \right)}
\end{align*}

That's messy, but now that we have a $T_2$. Then we use
$\rho_2 = \rho_1 \left( T_2 / T_1 \right)^{2/n}$ to compute a new
density (this was the change from the previous derivation).
@fig-isobar2507 shows the isobar at $P=0.1075$, which is near the
transition at $1/\pi$ density (see @fig-pvske_eta).

![Isobar at $P=0.1075$, the pressure near the transition at $1/\pi$
density (see @fig-pvske_eta).](images/isobar2507.png){#fig-isobar2507}

With temperature as the independent variable, the isobar in
@fig-isobaravt2507 show the expanding area-per-particle as the
temperature increases.

![Isobar of @fig-isobar2507 with axes reversed (temperature as
independent variable). The expansion of the substance with temperature
while under constant pressure is
clear.](images/isobaravt2507.png){#fig-isobaravt2507}

Similar algebra yields the following for a constant temperature
(Isotherm). Since we are transforming to a constant temperature, we can
first compute the new density
$\rho_2 = \rho_1 \left( T_2 / T_1 \right)^{2/n}$. Then:

\begin{align*}
P_2 &= \frac{P_1 \rho_2 T_2}{\rho_1 T_1} \\
    &= \frac{P_1 \eta T_2^{1 + 2/n}}{\rho_1 T_1} \\
    &= \frac{P_1 \left(\rho_1 / T_1^{n/2}\right)T_2^{1 + 2/n} }{\rho_1 T_1} \\
    &= P_1 \left(\frac{T_2}{T_1}\right)^{1 + 2/n}
\end{align*}

If we have pre-computed the new density, we can stop at the first step
above, but sometimes we don't care about the density, and so the final
form is utilized (@fig-isotherm2507).

![Isotherm in the transition
region.](images/isotherm2507.png){#fig-isotherm2507}

# Heating and Cooling

## Equations

We start with the Verlet algorithm derivation:

$$x_{n + 1} = x_n + v_n \Delta t + \frac{1}{2} a_n \Delta t^2 \\
\text{where } v_n = \frac{x_{n + 1} - x_{n - 1}}{2 \Delta t}$$

substituting this into the equation and solving for $x_{n+1}$ a simple
result is obtained:

$$x_{n + 1} = 2 x_n - x_{n-1} + a_n \Delta t^2$$

If we let the acceleration be velocity dependent such that
$\alpha_n = a_n + \beta v_n$ we can derive the following:

\begin{align*}
x_{n + 1} &= x_n + v_n \Delta t + \frac{a_n  + \beta v_n}{2} \Delta t^2\\
   &= x_n + \frac{x_{n + 1} - x_{n - 1}}{2} + 
      \frac{a_n  + \beta \frac{x_{n + 1} - x_{n - 1}}{2 \Delta t}}{2} \Delta t^2\\
   &= x_n + \frac{1}{2} x_{n+1} - \frac{1}{2} x_{n-1} + \frac{1}{2}a_n \Delta t^2      + \frac{1}{4}\beta x_{n+1} \Delta t - \frac{1}{4}\beta x_{n-1} \Delta t
\end{align*}

This follows:

\begin{align*}      
x_{n + 1} (\frac{1}{2} - \frac{1}{4}\beta \Delta t) &= 
      x_n - \frac{1}{2} x_{n-1} + \frac{1}{2}a_n \Delta t^2 - 
         \frac{1}{4}\beta x_{n-1} \Delta t\\
x_{n + 1} (1 - \frac{1}{2}\beta \Delta t) &= 
      2x_n - x_{n-1} + a_n \Delta t^2 - \frac{1}{2}\beta x_{n-1} \Delta t\\
x_{n + 1} &= 
   \frac{2x_n - \left(1 + \frac{1}{2}\beta \Delta t \right)x_{n-1} + a_n \Delta t^2}
            {1 - \frac{1}{2}\beta \Delta t}
\end{align*}

This matches [@Levy1977] result and code, which used
`heat1 = 1 / (1 - beta * dt / 2)` and `heat2 = 1 + beta dt / 2` making
the update equation `xp1 = (2*xn - heat2 * xnm1 + an dt^2) * heat1`.
We'll stuff these in `MD2State` and expose the parameter to
`RunSystem()`, the idea being that only one run of heating will ever be
executed before many long runs to attain equilibrium (`RunSystem()` will
read a `.jld2` file and only make one execution).

While the average acceleration of the particles is zero, the average
speed, i.e., $\langle |v_i| \rangle$ is going to be the square root of
the temperature ($T=k_B \langle v^2 \rangle$ in two dimensions), and by
the above procedure, this will grow by a factor of $\beta \Delta t$
every time step. So, if the temperature (mean kinetic energy) is 0.01,
and $\beta = 0.01$ and $\Delta t = 0.01$, then after 1,000 steps, we
would expect the average speed to go from 0.1 to
`0.1*(1 + 0.01* 0.01)^1000 =` `r 0.1*(1 + 0.01* 0.01)^1000`, and the
temperature then to climb to 0.122.

## Heating/Cooling Runs

The ability to heat and cool was added 139 new runs were created by
heating or cooling the last execution of one of eight runs.
Specifically, `S3.0008, 0009, 0010, & 0011` were heated and
`S3.0043, 0044, 0045, &0046` were cooled. Each heating/cooling step
involved 1,000 steps with the heating cooling parameter $\beta = 0.01$
(for heating) or $\beta = -0.01$ (for cooling). Any linear momentum
built during the execution (a potential problem in heating) is removed
at the end of the execution. @fig-heatS3008007 is a record of the
heating of `S3.0008`.

![Heating run of
`S3.0008.0007`.](images/2025-09-13-10-47-44.png){#fig-heatS3008007}

Each of the eight initial runs were heated or cooled, run to equilibrium
or four million points, and then this was repeated until the cooler ones
had been heated above $T = 0.0208$ and the hot ones until cooled below
$T = 0.004$. The process resulted in different number of heating/cooling
steps for each initial run. @tbl-HCcollect shows the basic temperature
ranges of the collections.

::: {#tbl-HCcollect}
|   Run   | H/C Steps | Start T   | End T     |
|:-------:|:---------:|:----------|:----------|
| S3.0008 |    18     | 0.0040190 | 0.0205726 |
| S3.0009 |    17     | 0.0045004 | 0.0209742 |
| S3.0010 |    16     | 0.0049730 | 0.0208289 |
| S3.0011 |    16     | 0.0054471 | 0.0231253 |
| S3.0043 |    18     | 0.0192274 | 0.0037479 |
| S3.0044 |    18     | 0.0197882 | 0.0038612 |

the `Init` run used to start the collection.
:::

The heating and cooling required more intervention than is desired, as
each run had to be run to equilibrium before a new temperature change
could be started (we did not wish to heat or cool systems not in
equilibrium, although after 4M steps, we did it anyway). Furthermore,
the steps ultimately proved a bit too large through the transition
region. So while providing a wealth of new data, the now 224 runs
complicate rather than simplify the overall picture. More on that in a
moment.

## Diffusion

Code to estimate self diffusion was also added and each of the
heating/cooling runs had diffusion measured, adding 139 diffusion
measurements to 42 measured on the original `Init` collection, for 181
total measurements. The overall series is represented in
@fig-TransitionIHC below (`TE` is total energy, `rv` is relative
temperature variance, `D` is diffusion, `LogFp` the logarithm of the F
statistic of diffusion regressions, `psiavg` the absolute value of the
complex average of the Nelson-Halperin parameter, `psiabs` the average
of the absolute value of hte parameter,
$C_v = 1 / \left( 1 - \frac{N \left< (\delta T)^2 \right>}{T^2} \right)$
(where $N$ is the number of particles, and $\left< (\delta T)^2 \right>$
is the temperature variance) is the specific heat, and `Log(Cv)` is the
logarithm of the specific heat calculated by taking the first difference
of temperature vs. energy computed for `Init` and each of the eight
`hseries`.

![Statistics around transition plotted against temperature. Circles are

# Improving Initialization

The super-heated and super-cooled runs produced by the heating and
cooling runs begged the question about initialization with all particles
in their minimum potential energy positions. This is rather like racking
the pool balls and giving them all an initial random velocity (rather
than only hitting the cue ball): it is an unusual part of the phase
space to say the least. While it appears to thermalize quickly, there is
a dependence between the runs which could skew the data. Therefore, a
considerable effort was made to randomize the starting positions. The
basic idea was to recognize a single particle as small part of the
overall system of $N$ particles (256 in our simulations so far). This
particle will have both potential and kinetic energy, and we will focus
only on its potential energy. The derivation below follows Reif
[@Reif1965 section 6.2] almost word-for-word.

## Derivation of Energy Distribution

Let The potential energy of particle $i$ be $E_r$, the energy of the
rest of the system be $E_s$, and the total energy be $E_T$. Then we have

$$E_r + E_s = E_T$$ {#eq-ET}

When particle $i$ has potential energy $E_r$ the rest of the particles
(which now includes particle $i$'s kinetic energy) must have energy
$E_s = E_T - E_r$. If particle $i$'s potential energy is $E_r$ then it
is in a particular state $r$, and the rest of the system has the number
of states given by $\Omega_s(E_T - E_r)$. The probability that particle
$i$ is in state $r$ is therefore proportional to the number of states of
the rest of the system:

$$P_r = C \Omega_s(E_T - E_r)$$ {#eq-Pr}

Where $C$ is the normalizing constant such that $\sum_r{P_r} = 1$. Now
we can expand the logarithm of the number of states in a Taylor series

$$\ln[ \Omega_s(E_T - E_r)] = 
\ln[ \Omega_s( E_T)] - \frac{\partial \ln( \Omega_s)}{\partial E_s}E_r + 
\cdots$$ {#eq-Tay1}

Ordinarily, we like to make the assumption that $E_r$ is minuscule
relative to $E_T$, but in a 256 particle system, it is roughly 0.2%;
small but not negligible. Nevertheless, we ignore the other terms of the
Taylor series, and recognize the partial derivative as
$\frac{\partial \ln( \Omega_s)}{\partial E_s} \equiv \beta \equiv 1/kT$,
where $k$ is Boltzmann's constant, unity in our simulation. Therefore we
can re-write @eq-Tay1 as

\begin{align}
\ln[\Omega_s(E_T - E_r) &= \ln[\Omega_s(E_T)] - \beta E_r \\
\Omega(E_T - E_r) &= \Omega_s(E_T) e^{-\beta E_r}
\end{align}

So @eq-Pr is now $P_r = C'e^{-\beta E_r}$, where $C'$ is now normalizing
the probability so that it sums to unity. Of course, this is just the
exponential distribution, and the excess potential energies will be
drawn from that. The trick is finding the particle deviation from the
minimum potential energy. @fig-tdfield shows a plot of the field in
three dimensions.

![Three-D plot of the potential field of a particle with the parameters
of the simulation ($\rho=1/\pi$, $R_{skn}=2.5$, $n=5$). The minimum
field has a value of 0.15949. The field was clipped at a PE of
2.0.](images/2025-09-26_17-14-23.png){#fig-tdfield}

A contour plot of the same thing is below (@fig-cpfield). The field
appears more-or-less circular out to a PE of about 0.3 or so.

![Contour plot of
@fig-tdfield](images/2025-09-26_17-26-06.png){#fig-cpfield}

@fig-fieldlin below shows two paths in the field and two simple
equations for comparison. It looks like the $r^5$ matches moving toward
a particle, and the $r^2$ looks like it matches moving between
particles. Note that The `Pdx` curve is the maximum, as it approaches a
nearest neighbor particle directly, and `Pdy` is the minimum, as it
moves directly between nearest neighbors.

![Plots of the simple $r^5$ potential (blue line, mostly under the `Pdx`
curve), a simple $r^2$ potential (reddish-orange line), and the actual
*excess* potential (the minimum iz zero in these plots) of moving the
particle along the x-axis (i.e., toward the right particle; yellow `Pdx`
curve) and moving along the y-axis (i.e., between the two upper
particles; green `Pdy` curve). The three gray vertical dashed lines are
at $x = a/2$, $a$, and $3a/2$, where $a$ is the inter-particle spacing
at a density of $\rho=1/\pi$ ($a \approx 1.9$). The minimum of `Pdx` at
$x = 3a/2$ is the minimum between two adjacent particles, distinguished
from $x = 0$ which is the test particle's home
position.](images/2025-09-27_09-55-42.png){#fig-fieldlin}

The system under simulation appears to have a transition around
$T = 0.013$, which is also the per-particle average kinetic energy. The
equipartition theorem would require roughly the same amount of energy to
be in the excess PE. We will be looking at temperatures up to about
$T = 0.02$, and should have some headroom in the PE, so we can book 3
times the mean at that high temperature, or 0.06. With a minimum PE of
0.15949, the total PE would be about 0.175949. A zoom into the contour
plot of @fig-cpfield shows that at the ranges where the PE is below 0.2,
the field really only depends on the distance.

![Zoom into @fig-cpfield.](images/zcp.pdf){#fig-zcp}

Similarly, we can zoom into @fig-fieldlin where we introduce a new
function `rn2[]` in the *Mathematica* code. This function is simply the
field difference between two particles given by
$\mathrm{rn2}(x) = \left[ (a - x)^{-n} + (a + x)^{-n} - 2a^{-n} \right]/2$
where $a$ is the crystal inter-particle distance

![Plot of the relavent functions within the range of the PE in question.
The new `rn2[]` *Mathematica* function tracks the `Pdx` and `Pdy`
functions very well at this range.](images/pz2.pdf){#fig-pz2}

The procedure then is to generate exponentially distributed random
numbers (using *Julia*'s `randexp()` function which generates numbers
with a unity mean), scale them for the desired temperature (by simply
multiplying each random number by the desired temperature), and then use
the *Julia* `Roots.jl` package `find_zero()` function to find the $x_i$
value such that $\mathrm{rn2}(x_i) = \epsilon_i$, where $\epsilon_i$ is
the random energy assigned to particle $i$. We ignore the issue that the
particle deviation is computed based on all other particles being in
their lattice positions. Once we have the deviations, we assign a random
angle to each particle, and place it at that $r, \theta$.

We quickly found that ignoring the adjacent displacements had an effect,
which was to generate PEs that were too high. Subsequently we scaled the
temperature down (by a factor of 2) and that seemed to work. @fig-T4b10
shows the initial execution at an initialization temperature of 0.01.

![Initialization with PE and KE set by the temperature. The `tfudge`
parameter was set to 0.5, so the PE was set by an average energy of
0.005. It can be seen that both the PE and the TE start near their
eventual settled energy. The *ringing* is likely due to the PE being
completely independent of the KE for each particle (one might expect
particles with very high PE to have low KEs, at least in the direction
of the nearest particle), thus the system is in an odd state, though not
as odd as the minimum PE state.](images/T4b10.png){#fig-T4b10}

## Series 4

The `S3` and `S3b` series only differed in how much energy was placed
into kinetic energy (KE) (the `b` version generated $2N$ random numbers
and then multiplied them by a factor to set the KE to the requested
target). The potential energy (PE) was always at its minimum. This
appears valid, as even in the transition region (`S3.00295` was
diffusing; see @fig-S3.295all). The KE quickly (200 steps) gives up its
initial value of 0.0264 to settle around 0.013022, while it rings for a
short while, by the end of the first 1,000 steps it has settled down.

![Plot of first execution of `S3.00295`. The KE and PE can be seen to
settle down quickly.](images/fig-S3.295all.png){#fig-S3.295all}

@fig-S3.295z is a zoom into the kinetic energy panel of fig-S3.295all.

![Zoom into @fig-S3.295all. The solid line is the final average of the
run computed over 4,999k steps (only the first 1k steps were
skipped).](images/fig-S3.295z.png){#fig-S3.295z}

Series four will focus on the single precision (`Float32`) data and time
step of $\tau = 0.0177737$, which is close to what was used in 1979 (it
was somewhere between 0.0178315 and the above). The first step is to do
a `revtest()` with `Float32` and the higher time step. We choose to
initialize at a temperature of $T=0.03$ as it is hotter than we plan to
run.

## Testing with `revtest()`

The RMS particle error `r sqrt(12.138896/256)`, 11.4% of inter-particle
distance, is given by $\sqrt{\delta_i^2/N}$, where $\delta_i$ is the
difference between particle $i$'s position before and after moving 1,000
steps forward and reverse, and $N$ is the number of particles. Here are
some example returns. @tbl-revtest shows the results.

::: {#tbl-revtest}
| Name     | 64/32 | $\tau$    | RMS Dist. | \% Lattice | Max Part. |
|:---------|:-----:|:----------|:----------|:-----------|:----------|
| F64      |  64   | 0.01      | 0.0142    | 0.749      | 0.04169   |
| F64013   |  64   | 0.013     | 0.0366448 | 1.92       | 0.176     |
| F640177  |  64   | 0.0177737 | 0.14517   | 7.6218     | 0.37303   |

It is evident that the error is not sensitive to the precision, but very
sensitive to the time step. We also point out that a run with the larger
time step but an initialization temperature of $T=0.2$ had an RMS error
of 0.0357 which is 1.876% of the lattice spacing (less than a quarter of
that at the higher temperature).

## Executing the Series

In spite of the the higher RMS error, we executed the series with the
higher time step and in `Float32` anyway. We created 163 runs, and
immediately ran into trouble with Energy and momentum growth. We did a
lot of work on energy growth with non-valid runs (it sort of appeared
that runs not declared valid, that is, those with a temperature trend,
had energy or momentum growth, or both). This turned out not to be the
case, and was a lot of wasted effort.

However, the energy and momentum growth, which was really only related
to the number of steps, could not be tolerated, so we had to create a
Velocity Verlet algorithm to update the particles. The details of this
algorithm are contained in **MD Notes 4.pdf**.

## Pair Distribution Function

In December of 2025, the `PairDist.jl` set of subroutines was added to
the *Julia* code base. These functions process saved `MDRecord` files to
estimate the pair distribution function $G_6(r)$ [@Gasser2010].

$$G_6(|\vec{r}_i - \vec{r}_j|) = \langle g_6(\vec{r}_i)g_6^*(\vec{r}_j)\rangle $$

where

$$g_6(\vec{r}_i) = 
\frac{1}{K_{nn}}\sum_{k=1}^{K_{nn}} e^{-i6\theta_{jk}}$$ {#eq-g6ri}

where $g_6$ measures the angle $\theta_{jk}$ between particle $i$ and
its $K_{nn}$ nearest neighbors (i.e., $k$ here is the *k*'th nearest
neighbor, not particle $k$). Since we have a constant density, we define
these nearest neighbors **not** with Voronoi cells [@Aurenhammer1991]
but as those within a ring half-way between the nearest neighbor
distance $a$ and the next-nearest neighbor (which is not at a distance
of $2a$ but $a\sqrt{3}$), so all particles within a radius of
$a(1 + \sqrt{3}) / 2$ (referred to as `NHOPr` in the `MD2` code).

The *Julia* function `avgpairdist()` will take a directory and a file
name base string, along with the number of files to process and the
number of bins in which to split values of $|\vec{r}_i - \vec{r}_j|$
into, and will then return a `tuple` of the bin width, the simple pair
count function (i.e., the average number of pairs at $r$), $G_6(r)$, the
average number of dislocations, and the standard deviation of that
average. The function can also plot those estimated functions.

```{julia}
#| eval: false
julia> MD2.avgpairdist(datadir, "S5b.00100*", 10, 100)
(fname, tfiles) = ("S5b.00100*.jld2", 32)
```

The output is not shown. The data is also written to the data directory
as `filebaseapd.csv`. The above code resulted in a file
`S5b.00100apd.csv`, and @fig-S5b100apd below.

![Log-log plots of pair distribution functions from
`S5b.00100apd.csv`.](images/S5b.00100apd.png){#fig-S5b100apd}

As of 1 May 2026, I am looking into the computation of $g_6(\vec{r}_i)$
in @eq-g6ri. To compute it for each particle, we walk through particles
by number from one to $N - 1$, and perform the sum for particle $i$, but
also for each particle $k > i$ that is in the set of $K_{nn}$ nearest
neighbors of particle $i$, as $\theta_{kj}  = \theta_{jk} - \pi$, and so
$e^{-i6\theta_{kj}} = e^{-i6(\theta_{jk} - \pi)} = e^{-i6\theta_{jk}} e^{i6\pi} = e^{-i6\theta_{jk}}$.
So, once we have $e^{-i6\theta_{jk}}$ we can add it to $g_6(\vec{r}_i)$
and also to $g_6(\vec{r}_k)$. By the time we have finished with particle
number $N - 1$, we will have computed all the $g_6$ values.

The way we estimate this function is to first estimate the number of
particles at range $r$, which we call $G(r)$. To estimate $G(r)$, we
define an array `P[i]` of $N_g$ bins with each bin representing
$\Delta r =$ `min( bx, by) / Ng`, and then walk through all particle
pairs, computing the distance $r_{ij}$ between the two particles, and
add a count to the array location given by `floor( r / dr) + 1`, where
`dr`$= \Delta r$. Thus, two particles nearly touching would be in bin 1,
and particles separated by the max distance would be in bin $N_g$. (Note
that a particle farther than the max distance would soon be wrapped back
by periodic boundary conditions.) So each bin $i$ of the array counts
the particles in a swath of width $\Delta r$ starting at $(i-1)\Delta r$
and ending at $i \Delta r$ thus area
$\pi(i\Delta r)^2 - \pi \left[ \delta r (i - 1)\right]^2= (2i -1)\pi {\Delta r}^2)$.

The quantity should be further normalized by the density of particles,
i.e., the number of particles expected in the swath, such that for a
uniform distribution of particles, a normalized bin would be unity
(thus, a swath with fewer than uniform particles would be less than on1,
and one with a higer density would be greater than one). We will also
process this over a number of files $N_f$, and, finally, we will only
add one to a bin when we count it (although 2 would be account for
particle paris $i,j$ and $j,i$), so we will divide by half the number of
particles ($N_p/2$). So the normalization of bin `i`, would be
$2 / ( \Delta r^2 \pi N_p N_f (2i - 1)$. Now we have an estimate of
$G(r)$, and we can perform the same process to compute $G_6(r)$, except
instead of adding one for each particle pair, we compute and add the
$g_6$ products, and then normalize this complex sum by `P[i]`.

$G_6(r)$ is the expected value of the correlation between particle
nearest neighbor count and positions. As of 26 January 2026, the program
performs the estimate as below:

$$\langle G_6(r) \rangle = \frac{1}{N_f N_p} \sum_{i=1}^{N_f} \sum_{j=1}^{Np -1} \frac{1}{N_{r_{i,j}}}\sum_{k=1}^{N_{r_{i,j}}} g_6^{i,j} {g_6^*}^{i,k}$$ {#eq-G6est}

where $N_f$ is the number of files, $N_p$ the number of particles, and
$N_{r_{i,j}}$ is the number of particles at range $r$ from particle $j$,
$g_6^{i,j}$ is the NHOP for particle $j$ from file $i$, and $g_6^{i,k}$
is the NHOP of the $k$'th particle in the range $r$ from particle $j$.
This estimate will be lower if the orientation changes over time (i.e.,
over the files), and our procedure puts 5,000 steps or more between the
each file. The alternate form is to take the absolute value of the each
result by file.

### Expected Minimum of $|G_6|$ {#sec-g6expmin}

While true zero or very near zero values of $|G_6|$ occur, particularly
at small ranges, hot systems will have noisy values with random angles,
particularly at long ranges. There are two cases to consider in the
limit of completely uncorrelated $g_6(\vec{r}_j)$: one in which particle
$j$ has six evenly spaced nearest neighbors, and one in which there are
not six. With six neighbors, $|g_6| = 1$. If it is not six but evenly
spaced, it is zero. The worst case is if the angles between the
neighbors are random uniform around their evenly spaced positions of
$2 \pi / n$. In @eq-g6ri, $\theta_{jk} = (k-1)(2 \pi/n) + \xi_k$ where
$\xi_k$ is a normal random variable over with a standard deviation much
less than $\pi / n$. Each term in the sum has a magnitude of one, but
the real and imaginary parts of the sum appear normal with mean zero and
standard deviation of about 0.289 or variance about 0.0832 (empirically
derived from an *R* function defined as
`g6rn <- function(n) sum( exp( 12i*pi*rnorm(n)/n))/n` with `n = 6`; this
generates angular noise with a standard deviation approximately
$pi / 6$). The expected value of @eq-G6est ($G_6$) in the limit will be
the average of $N$ such complex normal variables. Each real and
imaginary part will then be normal with mean zero and standard deviation
$0.289 / \sqrt{N}$ therefore will have a Rayleigh distribution with mean
$0.289 \sqrt{(\pi/ 2N )}$. For $N = 70 * 8000$ that's about
`r 0.289*sqrt( pi / (2*70*8000))`.

## Finding the Peaks {#sec-findpeaks}

A search of the literature did not reveal much on the peaks of the pair
distribution function for a hexagonal lattice. @Kaatz2006 did the first
eight, and other than the multiples of the lattice spacing all were
roots of integers:
$\left[ \sqrt{3}, \sqrt{7}, \sqrt{12}, \sqrt{13} \right]$. We could do a
search in *Mathematica* of the exact locations of each ring of
particles, but it seems easier, and just as effective, to do the search
in programmatically. We started in *Julia*, but ended up in *R*. The
process starts with a simple filter that finds all points that are
simply greater than their neighbors to the left and right. This will
find all the real peaks, but produces many spurious peaks, especially in
the low parts of each lobe. This peaks are then repeatedly filtered to
remove peaks that are less than 1/c times the height of their
neighboring peaks (and we used `c = 2`). This last filter was repeated
until it stopped changing. @fig-S5b210pks shows the result.

![$G6$ with identified peaks from S5b.00210. An estimate of the minimum
resulting from random orientation is shown by the light blue dashed
line.](images/2026-06-03%2016-41-44.png){#fig-S5b210pks}

I was concerned about the number of points in the averages, and so
@fig-reg3 was created. Although `dr = 0.13135`, about 1/15th of the mean
inter-particle separation of `a = 1.90463`.

![Number of samples in each `dr` sized ring observed from 30 files of
`S5b.00200` in the computation of $\langle G_6(r) \rangle$. The x axis
of this plot is an integer running from 1 to $N_g = 100$ in steps of
`dr = 0.13135`.](../Archived%20Notes/2026-Init-files/2026-02-16_11-34-56.png){#fig-reg3
width="400"}

## Performing the Reqression

Now we are ready to perform the regressions. The three regimes we are
trying to detect are (@Keim2007) 1) $G_6(r) \sim c$, more or less
constant in the solid, 2) $G_6(r) \sim r^{-\eta_6(\beta)}$, an algebraic
decline in order in the hexatic fluid, and 3)
$G_6(r) \sim e^{-r/\xi_6(\beta)}$, an exponential decline is the fully
fluid state (both $\xi_6$ and $\eta_6$ are expected to be functions of
the inverse temperature $\beta$). Keim, et.al. estimated $\eta_6$ and
$\xi_6$ for all temperatures, and compared the resulting statistics of
the three possibilities. For simplicity's sake, we will forgo non-linear
regression or maximum-likelihood estimation and simply linearize the
data, the data being the estimate of $G_6(r)$ and $r$.

### Properly Weighted Regression {#sec-pwr}

So code was added to `avgpairdist()` to estimate the variance of each
sample of $\langle G_6(r) \rangle$. This is done file-by-file, but the
sums extend over all the files. Following the notation in @eq-G6est, we
sum the magnitude squared of the raw sums (see @eq-G6sqrd)

$$G_6^2(r) = \frac{1}{N_f N_p} \sum_{i=1}^{N_f} \left( \sum_{j=1}^{N_p -1} \frac{1}{N_{r_{i,j}}}\sum_{k=1}^{N_{r_{i,j}}} g_6^{i,j} {g_6^*}^{i,k} \right)^2$$ {#eq-G6sqrd}

The the variance of the estimate is computed as

$$\sigma^2_{G_6}(r) = G_6^2(r) - \left( G_6(r) \right)^2$$

We note though, that this is an estimate of the variance of a single
sample of $G_6(r)$, not the variance of the estimate. The difference is
that the estimate is the average of $N_fN_pN_{r_{i,j}}$ samples, and
this number varies by $r$ (see @fig-reg3). So, the variance of the
estimate will decrease with increasing number of samples
($\sigma^2_{\overline{X}} = \sigma^2_X/n$, see Theorem 2 of chapter7,
pg. 130, of @Hoel). So, we have

$$\sigma^2_{\langle G_6(r) \rangle} = \frac{\sigma^2_{G_6}(r)}{N_f N_p \left( \sum_{j=1}^{N_p -1} N_{r_{i,j}} \right)}$$

Remember that for each file, the number of particles in each ring
$r_i = i \delta r$ is different. The variance was computed and error
bars added to the plot at the end of `avgpairdist()`. @fig-gstd is a
plot of that standard deviation.

![Standard deviation of `S5b.00200` as a function of
$i = r/ \delta r$.](../Archived%20Notes/2026-Init-files/2026-02-27_12-41-41.png){#fig-gstd
width="400"}

After all that, *Julia* does not have a convenient way to use such
weights. `GLM`'s `lm()` function only uses sample counts. The weights
$w_i$ should be applied such that each point's squared error is
multiplied by that weight, as it is proportional to the reciprocal of
the variance (the variance of multiple samples). In our example, we have
standard deviation, so we can call the weights the reciprocal of the
standard deviation squared. Also, we are performing regression on the
logarithm of the the observations, so the variance of the logarithm will
be quite different. We used this simple trick:

$$w_{\text{ln}_i} = \frac{1}{ \left( \ln(y_i + \sigma_i) - \ln(y_i - \sigma_i)\right)^2}$$

where $w_{\text{ln}_i}$ is the weight of the $i$th observation, $y_i$ is
the $i$th observation of $\langle G_6(r) \rangle$, and $\sigma_i$ is the
observed standard deviation of that observation. In *R*'s `lm()`, the
weight is simply the reciprocal if the variance.

## Maximum Likelihod Estimation

It is also possible that the longer range values of
$\langle G_6(r) \rangle$ are simply corrupted by noise. We have been
using the magnitude of $\langle G_6(r) \rangle$ to allow for rotations
of the particle groups in the hexatic phase (as observed in run
`S2b.0027` \[see Semi-Final.pdf\]). We will assume that the points are
normally distributed with the measured variances as in @fig-gstd above.
The functions will either follow a constant trajectory (which we will
detect from the F-Test just as we did for temperature equilibrium). The
other two are simply normal distributions with means given by either
$ar^{-\eta_6}$ or $ae^{-r/\xi_6}$. The likelihood function to maximize
is the product of all the individual probabilities of the observation
triplets or $(r_i, \sigma_i, y_i)$.

$$\mathcal{L}(r_i,a,b) = \prod_{i=1}^N \frac{\exp \left[ -(y_i - f(r_i,a,b))^2 / \sigma_i^2 \right]}{\sqrt{2 \pi} \sigma_i}$$

where $f(r,a,b)$ is either $ar^{-b}$ or $ae^{-rb}$. We compute the
log-likelihood as the following (with the minus sign moved to the left
side of the equal sign):

$$-\ln \left( \mathcal{L}(r_i,a,b) \right) =  \sum_{i=1}^N \lbrace \left( y_i - f(r_i,a,b) \right) ^2/\sigma_i^2 + \ln(\sigma_i) + \ln(2\pi)/2\rbrace $$

Since they are constant, the last two terms
$\ln(\sigma_i) + \ln(2\pi)/2$ can be ignored. Expressed as a negative
logarithm, the function should be minimized. The procedure is to start
with a guess of $a$ & $b$, compute the function, and then use numerical
derivatives to minimize the function in terms of $a$ & $b$. Implemented
this in *Julia* with the code below, appended to the `regress.jl` file.

```{julia}
#| eval: false

function expfit( r, a, b)
   return a * exp( -r * b)
end

function powerfit( r, a, b)
   return a * r^(-b)
end

function normalll( x::Vector{T}, y::Vector{T}, s::Vector{T},
                   f::Function, guess::Vector{T}) where T <: Real
   s2 = s.^2
   function ll( p)
      a, b = p
      yhat = f.( x, a, b)
      return sum( ((y .- yhat) .^ 2) ./ s2)
   end
   res = optimize( ll, guess)
   return Optim.minimizer( res)
end
```

@fig-mll shows the results of this with maximum-likelihood and
linearized regression results.

![$G_6$ fits of `S5b.00200` with the maximum likelihood fits of the
power-law and the exponential law curves in dashed
lines.](../Archived%20Notes/2026-Init-files/2026-03-06%2016-02-59.png){#fig-mll
width="400"}

It is a bit hard to see, but the maximum likelihood fits are very close
to the properly weighted linear regression fits. The objective values,
i.e., the log-likelihoods, for the power-law and exponential fits were
-3.14 and -6.84 respectively, indicating that the power-law is still the
better fit. Incidentally, the power-law coefficient was 1.83 vs. the
regression's 1.79, and the exponential coefficient was 0.696 vs. the
regression's 0.693. The fits each took about 0.156s, most of which
(99.9%) was compile time.

Developing the error bounds of the maximum likelihood estimates will
take about as much time as it did to develop the estimates themselves.
That the properly weighted linearized regression results were so similar
to the ML results is an indication that that the linearized equations
are still approximately normally distributed, so the ML approach will be
abandoned for the weighted linear regression.

For the solid, a simple regression of the estimate against $r$ will tell
us if there is any slope to speak of. To detect the hexatic fluid, we
will perform a linear regression of the logarithm of the estimate
against the logarithm of the range:
$\ln\left( \langle G_6(r) \rangle \right) \sim a \ln(r) + b$, where $b$
is expected to be zero (or a constant for the experiment) and $a$ is an
estimator of $-\eta_6(\beta)$. For the fully fluid equation, we will
regress the log of the estimate against the range:
$\ln\left( \langle G_6(r) \rangle \right) \sim a r + b$, where $b$ will
be zero or a constant, and $a$ will estimate $-\xi_6(\beta)$. For each
of these regressions, we will want the coefficients, the standard error
of each coefficient, the correlation coefficient, and the F-statistic
data (value and degrees of freedom). Finally, we decided to use `nls()`
to fit the curves, and recorded the weighted residual squared error
divided by the number of degrees of freedom.

## Wrapping Up Series 5 Before Extending

By August of 2026, we have created the pair-distribution function, found
its peaks, and fit curves the three curves to the $G_6(r)$. What we
found is that the power-law formula usually has the best fit. We found
that the first few peaks are generally higher then the rest of the peaks
even for the coldest runs. However, we tried skipping the first two
points, and the power-law still were significant. See @fig-linpowexf:
only a subset of the hot runs exponential fits Reduced Squared Error
were less than the power-law fit.

![Comparing the three $G_6$ fits. Only some exponential fits beat the
power-law, and then only on systems above the critical total energy of
0.1441 (hot points; see below for description of this
energy).](images/2026-08-20%2007-52-51.png){#fig-linpowexf}

The exponential fits were not consistently better above a certain
temperature, but they were never better below the critical temperature
(@fig-rserat).

![Ratio of the power-law and exponential fits RSE. The vertical red
dashed line is the melting temperature of 0.013085. The horizontal blue
line is at the ratio of one: points with a ratio above one mean the
exponential fit is
better.](images/2026-08-22%2014-34-29.png){#fig-rserat}

Nevertheless, we computed the $\eta_6$ and $\xi_6$ coefficients from the
power-law and exponential fits (respectively) for all of the runs.
$\eta_6$ behaved pretty well, gradually rising until it hit 1/4 right at
the transition temperature.

![Log plot of values of $\eta_6$ estimated from power-law fits. Red
dashed vertical line is the transition temperature of 0.01309. The
horizontal dashed line is the critical value of
$\eta_6 = 1/4$.](images/2026-08-20%2009-20-44.png)

According to @Nelson1979, $\xi_6$ is a function of temperature:

$$\xi_6(T) \sim exp \left( \frac{b}{(T - T_m)^\nu} \right)$$ {#eq-xi6ot}

Where $T_m$ is the isotropic fluid transition temperature, and
$\nu = 0.36963$. This would only apply at temperatures higher than
$T_m$. We were able to fit the equation in two steps. We added an
overall multiplier (which evaluated to 1.3453) and $b$ fit to 0.062124.
We were not able to use *R* to fit $T_m$ (which is what @Keim2007 did)
as it would fail with a "`singular matrix`" error.

![Fit of @eq-xi6ot to $\xi_6$ estimates above transition temperature.
The vertical red dashed line is the transition temperature of 0.01309.
Note the point which this line crosses is not included in the
fit.](images/2026-08-21%2010-47-11.png){#fig-xi6fit2}

The dislocation density (really point defects as measured here) also
leads to a single transition. The point defects are simply particles
whose nearest neighbors as measured by counting particles within the
Nelson-Halperin distance: one half the distance between the nearest
neighbor and the next-nearest neighbor particles at the specified
density. This a distance $a(1+\sqrt{3})/2$ where $a$ is the
inter-particle distance of the solid at density $\rho$ given by
$a = \sqrt{2/\rho\sqrt{3}}$. @fig-dsmean shows the density of the point
defects measured.

![Mean Dislocation Count vs. total energy per partical. Blue points are
identically zero. Light gray bars show ±𝜎 observed dislocations. The
vertical red dashed line is at 0.1441$\epsilon$ from run `S5b.00123`.
The energy gap surrounding that point is 0.00105 on the lower side and
0.00083 on the upper side, about twice the average
step.](images/2026-08-22%2012-47-09.png){#fig-dsmean}

Due to the unique placement of the highlighted point, its parameters are
used as the critical point for total energy (0.1441) and temperature
(0.01309). We found a strong linear relationship between the dislocation
density and the excess total energy (the energy above the rest energy at
that density). This led to an expression (via linear regression) of the
dislocation density and temperature given by $D(E) = aE^b$, where we
found $a = 53.68$ and $b = 7.158$. A direct estimation of the parameters
via `lm( log( dsden) ~ log( t))` for the points with non-zero
dislocations and whose dislocation density was below that of run
`S5b.00123` (34.944) led to $a = 1.53 \times 10^{10}$ (which is
surprisingly large) and $b = 6.046$. @fig-ddvt shows the results of
these fits.

![Dislocation density vs. temeprature. The black fit line was the
original fit of disloaction density divided by execss energy and the red
fit line was the direct log-log fit of the non-zero points below a
dislocation count of 34.944. The horizontal lines are the predicted
dislocation density at the critical energy (black line) or temperature
(red line).](images/2026-08-22%2013-22-40.png){#fig-ddvt}

The lowest values of these graphs are samples in which there was one of
30 systems which had two dislocations (determined by the `dscount` of
30, the `dsmean` of 0.0667, and `dsstd` of 0.365: `dsmean*30` is 2, and
`dsstd^2` is 0.1333, which is twice `dsmean`, indicating a single
Poisson event of 2 dislocations).

### Specific Heat

Following section 7.7 of @Reif1965 we can predict the specific heat of
the solid form. In two dimensions, the sum in equation (7.7.1) would be
over $2N_a$ instead of $3N_a$. The theory is that at low enough
temperatures there are small lattice vibrations which are approximately
like simple springs. The molar specific heat is given by

$$E = \sum_{i=1}^{2N_a} \left( \frac{p_i^2}{2m} + 
            \frac{1}{2}\kappa_i q_i^2 \right)$$

where $N_a$ is Avogadro's number, $p_i$ is the momentum in the i'th
particle dimension, $m$ is the particle mass, $\kappa_i$ is the elastic
constant of the i'th particle dimension's spring, and $q_i$ is the
displacement in the i'th particle dimension from its home position.
Since both the potential and kinetic energy's are quadratic quantities,
the equipartition theorem applies to both, and
$p_i^2 / 2m = \kappa_iq_i^2 / 2 = kT / 2$, so that
$E = 2N_a(kT / 2)\times2 = 2N_akT$.

In our system, $m=1$, $k=1$, and the energies we use are per particle,
so the specific heat is per particle andd is given by:

$$c_v = \left( \frac{\partial E}{\partial T} \right)_v = 2$$

@fig-cvt is a plot of this for series `S5b`.

![Numerical derivative of energy with respect to temperature. The
vertical red dashed line is the transition temperature of
$T = 0.01309$.](images/2026-08-22%2017-30-06.png){#fig-cvt}

There does not appear to be a transition into the hexatic phase. Even
the coldest samples show a significant power-law regression fit to
$G_6$, as well as a significant linear fit. The small system size may
make it difficult to distinguish between a slowly declining $G_6$ and
one that has relaxed to constant. While the specific heat does show
something stating to happen around $T = 0.0075$, there are no other
distinguishing features that would indicate a fluid phase. Indeed, the
diffusion is non-existent below the transition energy. See the `lnFvald`
data item in @fig-g6statplt below.

![$G_6$ statistics alongside thermodynamic quantities. From top to
bottom, left to right, `lnxi6`, `lneta6`, and `lin.Estimate` are the
relevant coefficients of the exponential ($\ln(\xi_6)$), power-law
($\ln(\eta_6$), and linear fits, respectively. `lnexfRSE`, `lnpowRSE`,
and `lnlinRSE` are the logarithm of the respective RSEs. `lnFvald` is
the logarithm of the diffusion regression F-Statistic, `rtv` the
relative temperature variance, and `dsmean` is the mean dislocation
count. The red vertical line is at the transition energy
$E_t = 0.1441\epsilon$.](images/2026-08-25%2009-19-48.png){#fig-g6statplt}

## Finishing Seris 5 Runs

By the end of September, I decided to execute all runs to 2M steps.
Complete heating and cooling runs were made spanning the transition
region, and this was completed on 28 September 2026. @fig-S5S5b is a
plot of the all that data (plot taken from [S5
Finish.pdf](../Archived%20Notes/S5%20Finish.pdf). Series `S5b` now has
654 samples: 110 initialized and 272 heated, and 272 cooled, both with
four series.

From top to bottom, left to right, @fig-S5S5b shows Temperature,
Pressure, Diffusion(`D`), `LogFpD` is the common logarithm of the
diffusion F-statistic probability value (the probability that the
regression occurs randomly; note that many values are smaller than
$10^{-15}$), `psiavg` is $|\langle \psi_6 \rangle|$ (the magnitude of
the complex average) and `psiabs` is $\langle |\psi_6| \rangle$ (the
average of the magnitudes), `dsmean` is the mean number of dislocations
(`S5b` only), `Cv` is the specific heat computed as
$C_v = 1 / \left( 1 - N  \sigma_T^2 / T^2 \right)$, where $N$ is the
number of particles (256) and $\sigma_T^2 / T^2$ is the relative
temperature variance (`rtv`), `logEta6` is the logarithm of $\eta_6$
(i.e., the power-law estimate of $G_6$ decay), and finally `rseRatio`,
which is the ratio of the $G_6$ power-law and exponential fits residual
standard errors (the ratio being less than one means that the power-law
fit was better).

![Key statistics for the complete series `S5` & `S5b` and `S5b`s heating
and cooling runs. See text for description of
data.](images/2026-10-05%2017-00-02.png){#fig-S5S5b}
